title: Pelvic Binder Placement & Hemorrhage Control
keywords: level matters more than tightness, the binder goes over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests, a binder placed too high barely reduces the fracture at all
don't log roll a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture to place the binder, minimize movement and slide it into place
a binder is a temporizing measure, not a cure, it buys time for resuscitation and definitive management, it doesn't replace angio-embolization or surgical fixation for ongoing bleeding
apply based on mechanism and clinical suspicion, don't wait for a pelvic X-ray to confirm the fracture before binding an unstable-mechanism, hemodynamically concerning patient
sources: Bonner TJ, et al. Accurate placement of a pelvic binder improves reduction of unstable fractures of the pelvic ring. Injury. 2011;42(10):1015-1019.

purpose: Correct placement level and technique for a pelvic binder — a temporizing hemorrhage-control measure for a suspected unstable pelvic fracture, buying time for definitive resuscitation and management.
entryPrompt: Apply based on mechanism and clinical suspicion — do not wait for a pelvic X-ray to confirm a fracture before binding a hemodynamically concerning patient with a mechanism consistent with pelvic injury.

nodes.body:
Suspect an unstable pelvic fracture in blunt trauma (especially high-energy mechanisms — motor vehicle collision, motorcycle, fall from height, pedestrian struck) with:
- pelvic pain
- pelvic instability on gentle exam
- unexplained hemodynamic instability after trauma

Do NOT repeatedly spring/rock the pelvis to test for instability — this can dislodge an early clot and worsen bleeding. A single gentle assessment (or skipping mechanical testing entirely in favor of imaging/binding based on mechanism) is preferred over repeated manipulation.

nodes.prompt: 2. Minimize movement while placing the binder
nodes.body: Do NOT log roll a patient with a suspected unstable pelvic fracture to place the binder — this can worsen displacement and bleeding. Instead, carefully slide the binder underneath the patient with minimal movement, or use a scoop stretcher / coordinated log-lift technique if the binder must go underneath, minimizing pelvic motion throughout.

nodes.prompt: 3. Position at the correct LEVEL — greater trochanters, not the iliac crests
nodes.body:
This is the single most common placement error and the one that matters most: the binder must sit at the level of the GREATER TROCHANTERS (roughly the level of the pubic symphysis anteriorly), NOT higher up at the iliac crests.

A binder placed too high provides dramatically less fracture reduction — studies show the fracture gap can be nearly 3x larger when a binder is placed above the trochanteric level compared to correct placement.

If you're unsure, palpate the greater trochanters directly and align the binder there.

Align the binder symmetrically on both sides before tightening — an asymmetric binder can worsen rather than reduce a fracture.
- Tighten firmly and evenly per the device's instructions (commercial pelvic binders typically have a mechanism indicating adequate tension).
- A bedsheet-improvised binder should be snugged firmly and secured (tied/clamped), but avoid excessive tension that could cause skin injury, especially with prolonged use.

A binder is a TEMPORIZING measure, not a definitive treatment. It buys time by stabilizing the fracture and reducing pelvic volume (which helps tamponade venous/cancellous bone bleeding), but it does NOT control arterial bleeding from a major vessel injury.
- Continue standard hemorrhage-control resuscitation (see hemorrhagic-shock-mtp) in parallel.
- Get trauma surgery/interventional radiology involved promptly for definitive management (angio-embolization for arterial bleeding, or surgical fixation).

Do not treat binder placement as having solved the problem.

checklist: Movement minimized while placing the binder — no log rolling a suspected unstable pelvis
Binder positioned at the level of the GREATER TROCHANTERS, not the iliac crests
Symmetric placement confirmed on both sides before final tightening
Understood as a temporizing measure — hemorrhage-control resuscitation and definitive management (angio-embolization/surgical fixation) pursued in parallel, not deferred
